Days 1 and 2 are built. Day 3 moves from reading an estimate to reviewing the
evidence used for a decision. Keep 60/60/75 minutes, one GreenWaste case,
two-sided participant sheets and one short trainer demonstration per session.
No participant coding. The tables below are the next daily approval boundary
required by `HANDOFF.md`.

## Session 1 Judge a value for money claim

| Screen | Participant task | Minutes |
|---|---|---:|
| 1 A saving is not the whole decision | Recall a credible result and ask what costs are missing | 4 |
| 2 Read the ratio claim | Predict approval and give a reason before opening assumptions | 4 |
| 3 Open what went into it | Identify saving source, programme cost and duration | 5 |
| 4 Read the result at today's value | One trainer calculation; interpret benefits divided by costs | 5 |
| 5 A saving next year | Read a simple timeline; explain why later benefits count less | 5 |
| 6 What costs were left out | Flag omitted staff and business costs in an extract | 6 |
| 7 Predict your scenario | Groups use Fiona's scenario cards and commit a prediction | 8 |
| 8 Put it on the ratio wall | Reveal scenario result; post prediction and result on existing A1 board | 7 |
| 9 What could flip the decision | Name the assumption doing most work and ask for evidence | 6 |
| 10 Repair an AI recommendation | Remove an unconditional value-for-money assurance | 6 |
| 11 Your question from memory | Individual question and purpose | 4 |

Use the corrected DiD estimate as an explicitly provisional benefit input;
its causal limitations carry forward. Programme costs, duration and discount
rate are fictional assumptions, labelled as such. Recompute the headline and
scenario cards from one model. Preserve the ratio wall, separate prediction
and result lanes, and eight group scenario allocations. Limit the main route
to a few decision-relevant assumptions; remove repeated sliders and full grids.

## Session 2 Read a chart before trusting its story

| Screen | Participant task | Minutes |
|---|---|---:|
| 1 Which picture would you use | Choose and explain before opening chart labels | 4 |
| 2 Same values different axes | Toggle axis range; inspect values rather than shape | 6 |
| 3 Mark up the chart | Individual source, units, comparison and uncertainty check | 7 |
| 4 What an average hides | Open a distribution; identify who the average misses | 6 |
| 5 A percentage of what | Use GreenWaste landfill totals and business averages; one trainer calculation | 7 |
| 6 Read an effect and its interval | Compare a point estimate with the decision rule | 6 |
| 7 Choose and repair | Pairs fix one misleading chart and write a caption | 10 |
| 8 Check an AI caption | Match each sentence to visible chart evidence | 6 |
| 9 Defend your chart choice | State what a reader could and could not conclude | 4 |
| 10 Your question from memory | Individual question and purpose | 4 |

Keep three focused habits: inspect scales and labels, inspect what is averaged,
and inspect comparison and uncertainty. Remove the school-zone case, pie-chart
detour and repeated discount-rate lesson. The percentage task uses GreenWaste
landfill quantities; explain the denominator instead of treating differently
weighted averages as interchangeable. Native toggles need prediction and
feedback; room voting remains optional with a paper fallback.

## Session 3 Question the analyst

| Screen | Participant task | Minutes |
|---|---|---:|
| 1 Would you sign this note | Read a short recommendation and commit individually | 4 |
| 2 Locate its evidence | Identify estimates, populations and the selected headline | 5 |
| 3 Choose three useful questions | Work alone with the shortened QA sheet | 6 |
| 4 Improve a vague question | Rewrite it to request evidence that could affect the decision | 5 |
| 5 Prepare for the clinic | Groups rank questions and nominate a spokesperson | 7 |
| 6 Break | Five-minute break | 5 |
| 7 Ask the analyst | Groups ask; trainer answers from a fixed source-backed answer bank | 14 |
| 8 Open one requested result | One short trainer demonstration tied to the chosen question | 6 |
| 9 Score the answers | Supported, partial or unanswered; cite the source | 6 |
| 10 Identify what remains | Choose the unresolved issue most likely to change the decision | 5 |
| 11 Revisit sign-off | Individual decision and reason, then compare with opening choice | 5 |
| 12 Check an AI review | Repair source errors and unsupported approval language | 4 |
| 13 Your request to the evaluator | Write a short specific evidence request independently | 3 |

The clinic preserves participant-led questioning. The answer bank must agree
with the corrected pilot-and-city data and disclose missing evidence. It must
not fabricate earlier trends, attrition or a score-manipulation check. Retire
the old neighbourhood lab from this teaching route. Keep further analyses as
optional trainer detail; one result is produced live. Compare reasons before
and after, while judging learning from individual written evidence requests.

## Build and review

After approval, rebuild the three decks, participant sheets, scenario cards,
trainer keys, QA answer bank and exercise brief together. Render every deck,
exercise controls and trainer outputs, and inspect every print page. Publish
unlinked previews. Day 4 remains two course-owned sessions; the final slot is
the other provider's evaluation simulation.
